title: Parallel Teleportation via AME(5,2) States on IBM Quantum Hardware
abstract: The five-qubit Absolutely Maximally Entangled AME$(5,2)$ state, whose every pair of qubits is maximally mixed so that all its information lives in non-local correlations, could in principle serve as a single shared quantum networking resource for teleporting two unknown qubits in parallel (each via its own Bell measurement and Pauli correction). Nonetheless, its hardware implementations remain scarce despite its theoretical importance. Here, we demonstrate parallel teleportation based on a five-qubit absolutely maximally entangled state, AME$(5,2)$, on the superconducting processor ibm_pittsburgh. We construct three-qubit Clifford decoders that extract two Bell pairs using three logical two-qubit gates for each of 60 inequivalent sender-receiver assignments. Using parallelization and classical Pauli frame post-processing, we retain reference-receiver entanglement on both channels after three teleportation rounds. With XY4 dynamical decoupling and the lowest-cost decoder, the final entanglement fidelities are $0.704\pm0.028$ and $0.680\pm0.022$, where uncertainties are pointwise $99\%$ confidence-interval half-widths over eight trials. Their lower bounds exceed the separability threshold of $1/2$. The decoder with lower circuit depth generally retains higher mean fidelity, and XY4 generally improves on XX. These results establish a hardware demonstration of two-channel entanglement transmission through repeated AME-assisted teleportation and provide compact decoding circuits for reconfigurable multipartite communication.
summary: This paper reports a hardware demonstration of parallel quantum teleportation using the AME(5,2) state on superconducting quantum hardware. By implementing optimized decoding circuits and utilizing classical post-processing, the authors successfully maintained entanglement fidelity across multiple teleportation rounds. This work advances the practical realization of multi-channel quantum communication protocols.
main_problem: The paper aims to demonstrate the feasibility of parallel quantum teleportation using a single, highly entangled resource state, the AME(5,2), on real quantum hardware.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated entanglement retention across two parallel channels over three teleportation rounds, achieving final fidelities exceeding the separability threshold of 1/2.
method: The experiment involves constructing and implementing optimized Clifford decoders to extract multiple Bell pairs from the AME state, followed by parallel teleportation rounds and classical Pauli frame post-processing.
model_or_system: The resource is the five-qubit Absolutely Maximally Entangled AME(5,2) state. The physical platform used for the demonstration is the superconducting processor, specifically the ibm_pittsburgh quantum hardware.
key_observables: Final entanglement fidelities ($0.704 \pm 0.028$ and $0.680 \pm 0.022$), signed Bell correlations ($\langle XX angle$, $-\langle Y Y angle$, $\langle ZZ angle$), and circuit execution time.
important_parameters: Three teleportation rounds; the separability threshold of 1/2; the use of XY4 dynamical decoupling.
main_assumptions: The fidelity measurements include state preparation and measurement errors, and the comparison between classical and real-time Pauli correction methods is complicated by differing experimental acquisitions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the joint and separate operations for AME(5,2)-assisted parallel teleportation, show implemented decoder circuits (Rank 1, Rank 58), and compare entanglement fidelity decay across multiple rounds under various error mitigation and decoupling schemes.
paper_structure: The paper details the theoretical basis of AME states, presents the experimental setup on the IBM hardware, describes the decoder construction and optimization, and finally reports comparative results on entanglement fidelity retention across multiple rounds using different error mitigation and decoding strategies.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, hardware-validated demonstration of complex quantum networking protocols (parallel teleportation) using advanced multipartite entangled states, which is highly relevant for building scalable quantum repeaters and communication channels.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Two directions of AME(5, 2)-assisted parallel teleportation (n = 5, d = 2, m = 2), following Helwig et al. [12]. (a) Joint senders to separate receivers; (b) sep- arate senders to joint receivers. The shaded three-qubit group performs joint decoding; the dashed group acts lo- cally. Resource qubits sA, sB are Bell-measured with in- puts IA, IB, yielding outputs OA, OB on receivers rA, rB, respectively; ℓis disentangled and unused. Colours dis- tinguish channels; arrows indicate input-state transfer. Bell measurements, classical communication and Pauli corrections or frame updates are implicit.

FIG. 2. Illustration of the role assignment (sA → rA, sB →rB). The source set {sA, sB} bypasses V ; the decoder acts jointly on the remaining three AME qubits to produce rA, rB and the disentangled qubit ℓ. Dashed arrows indicate teleportation of inputs sup- plied at the source sites to the assigned receivers. Bell measurements, classical communication and Pauli cor- rections are implicit. Assigning the five qubits to the ordered roles (sA, rA, sB, rB, ℓ) gives 5! = 120 labelled assignments; identifying assignments that differ only by exchanging the two channel labels leaves 120/2 = 60.

FIG. 3. The logical decoder circuits, read from left to right. Only the three active AME qubits are displayed; the two source qubits bypass the decoder. Filled circles and ⊕denote CNOT controls and targets. Both decoders contain three CNOTs. Rank 1 contains three Hadamards, one S and one S† gate; rank 58 contains six Hadamards, two S, three S† and two X gates. Their depths are six and ten, respectively, counting sequential layers of all gates while allowing independent operations on disjoint qubits to share a layer.

FIG. 4. Circuit diagram of one logical round of parallel teleportation, using the rank 1 decoder. At R0, the H-CNOT circuits prepare (RA, IA) and (RB, IB) in |Φ+⟩. The references RA, RB are retained while V014 decodes the AME resource. Bell outcomes (uc, vc) determine the Pauli correction on Oc. The displayed correction boxes are implemented through classical Pauli frame post-processing in the main experiment. In the cascade, I(R+1) c ≡O(R) c . The same reference qubits are retained through the cascade. The diagram shows logical operations, not their parallelised hardware schedule.

FIG. 5. Reference-receiver entanglement fidelities after repeated AME-assisted parallel teleportation on hardware, with optimisation level 2 and classical Pauli frame post-processing. Panels (a) and (b) show channels A and B. Blue circles and orange squares identify ranks 1 and 58; solid filled-marker curves show XY4, and dashed open-marker curves show XX. Points are M3-mitigated means over eight trials; error bars are pointwise two-sided 99% confidence intervals. The thick black dotted line marks the 1/2 separability threshold, and R0 is the input Bell pair baseline. The data are obtained from the full grouped-bar results in Supplementary Material, Sec. VII.
